claim: Vascular endothelial cells (ECs) derived from the central nervous system (CNS) variably lose their unique barrier properties during in vitro culture.
source: Vascular endothelial cells (ECs) derived from the central nervous system (CNS) variably lose their unique barrier properties during in vitro culture, hindering the development of robust assays for blood-brain barrier (BBB) function, including drug permeability and extrusion assays.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known phenomenon that motivates the study.

claim: Loss of CNS EC barrier properties during culture hinders the development of robust assays for blood-brain barrier (BBB) function, including drug permeability and extrusion assays.
source: Vascular endothelial cells (ECs) derived from the central nervous system (CNS) variably lose their unique barrier properties during in vitro culture, hindering the development of robust assays for blood-brain barrier (BBB) function, including drug permeability and extrusion assays.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of the loss of barrier properties in culture.

claim: Standard culture conditions are associated with a rapid and selective loss of BBB transcripts and chromatin features in mouse CNS ECs.
source: We observe that standard culture conditions are associated with a rapid and selective loss of BBB transcripts and chromatin features, as well as a greatly reduced level of beta-catenin signaling.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the comparison of acutely isolated versus cultured CNS ECs using RNA-seq and ATAC-seq.

claim: Standard culture conditions are associated with a greatly reduced level of beta-catenin signaling in mouse CNS ECs.
source: We observe that standard culture conditions are associated with a rapid and selective loss of BBB transcripts and chromatin features, as well as a greatly reduced level of beta-catenin signaling.
evidence: This is a primary finding based on analysis of beta-catenin-responsive gene expression and chromatin accessibility.

claim: Forced expression of a stabilized derivative of beta-catenin has little or no effect on gene expression or chromatin accessibility in vitro.
source: Interestingly, forced expression of a stabilized derivative of beta-catenin, which in vivo leads to a partial conversion of non-BBB CNS ECs to a BBB-like state, has little or no effect on gene expression or chromatin accessibility in vitro.
evidence: This is a primary finding from comparing WT and beta-catenin stabilized cultured CNS ECs.

claim: Forced expression of stabilized beta-catenin in vivo leads to a partial conversion of non-BBB CNS ECs to a BBB-like state.
source: Interestingly, forced expression of a stabilized derivative of beta-catenin, which in vivo leads to a partial conversion of non-BBB CNS ECs to a BBB-like state, has little or no effect on gene expression or chromatin accessibility in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Vascular endothelial cells (ECs) develop unique cellular and molecular properties to meet the specialized needs of target tissues.
source: Vascular endothelial cells (ECs) develop unique cellular and molecular properties to meet the specialized needs of target tissues (Augustin and Koh, 2017; Potente and Mäkinen, 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: In the CNS vasculature, ECs acquire a set of properties that collectively form the blood-brain barrier (BBB) or its retinal equivalent, the blood-retina barrier (BRB).
source: In the central nervous system (CNS) vasculature, the object of study here, ECs acquire a set of properties that collectively form the blood-brain barrier (BBB) or its retinal equivalent, the blood-retina barrier (BRB).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about CNS EC specialization.

claim: The unique CNS EC phenotype arises from a genetic regulatory program that suppresses the production of fenestrae- and caveolae-associated components.
source: This unique EC phenotype arises from a genetic regulatory program that (1) suppresses the production of fenestrae- and caveolae-associated components, thereby reducing intra-endothelial diffusion and transcytosis, respectively
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: Suppression of fenestrae- and caveolae-associated components reduces intra-endothelial diffusion and transcytosis in CNS ECs.
source: This unique EC phenotype arises from a genetic regulatory program that (1) suppresses the production of fenestrae- and caveolae-associated components, thereby reducing intra-endothelial diffusion and transcytosis, respectively
evidence: This is stated as a mechanistic consequence of the genetic regulatory program.

claim: The BBB genetic regulatory program enhances the production of tight junction proteins that block intercellular diffusion.
source: and (2) enhances the production of tight junction proteins that block intercellular diffusion, transporters that carry small molecules such as glucose and amino acids from the blood to the brain parenchyma, and efflux pumps that extrude toxic molecules from the brain parenchyma (Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as part of the BBB genetic program with a supporting citation.

claim: The BBB genetic regulatory program enhances the production of transporters that carry small molecules such as glucose and amino acids from the blood to the brain parenchyma.
source: and (2) enhances the production of tight junction proteins that block intercellular diffusion, transporters that carry small molecules such as glucose and amino acids from the blood to the brain parenchyma, and efflux pumps that extrude toxic molecules from the brain parenchyma (Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as part of the BBB genetic program with a supporting citation.

claim: The BBB genetic regulatory program enhances the production of efflux pumps that extrude toxic molecules from the brain parenchyma.
source: and (2) enhances the production of tight junction proteins that block intercellular diffusion, transporters that carry small molecules such as glucose and amino acids from the blood to the brain parenchyma, and efflux pumps that extrude toxic molecules from the brain parenchyma (Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as part of the BBB genetic program with a supporting citation.

claim: Numerous studies have found that cultured ECs have a propensity to lose their tissue-specific properties.
source: Numerous studies have found that cultured ECs have a propensity to lose their tissue-specific properties (DeLeve et al., 2004; Durr et al., 2004; Lacorre et al., 2004; Sellaro et al., 2007; March et al., 2009; Burridge and Friedman, 2010; Géraud et al., 2010; Kim and Rajagopalan, 2010; Tasnim and Zink, 2012; Urich et al., 2012; Uhlig et al., 2014; Zhao et al., 2014; reviewed in Helms et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with extensive citations.

claim: An EC culture system that could faithfully reproduce the small molecule permeability, transport, and extrusion properties of the BBB would permit high throughput in vitro screening of drug candidates to predict their brain penetration.
source: An EC culture system that could faithfully reproduce the small molecule permeability, transport, and extrusion properties of the BBB would permit high throughput in vitro screening of drug candidates to predict their brain penetration (Helms et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a practical application with a supporting citation.

claim: Loss of the CNS EC-specific expression profile by cultured brain ECs could result from a loss of brain-specific signaling, including beta-catenin signaling.
source: Loss of the CNS EC-specific expression profile by cultured brain ECs could result from a loss of brain-specific signaling, including beta-catenin signaling (also called canonical Wnt signaling).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis based on the context of the study.

claim: Conditional deletion of beta-catenin signaling components in ECs in vivo leads to loss of BBB-specific gene expression.
source: Conditional deletion of beta-catenin signaling components in ECs in vivo leads to loss of BBB-specific gene expression (Liebner et al., 2008; Stenman et al., 2008; Daneman et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2014; Cho et al., 2017; Hupe et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with multiple supporting citations.

claim: Elevating beta-catenin signaling in ECs in vivo leads to a partial conversion of highly permeable ECs in the circumventricular organs (CVOs) and choroid plexus to a BBB state.
source: Conversely, elevating beta-catenin signaling in ECs in vivo leads to a partial conversion of highly permeable ECs in the circumventricular organs (CVOs) and choroid plexus to a BBB state (Benz et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Primary cultures of young adult (8–16 week) brain ECs were grown in standard EC culture medium for eight days.
source: To acquire an unbiased, genome-wide view of the effect of in vitro culture on the transcriptional and chromatin landscapes of CNS ECs, we grew primary cultures of young adult (8–16 week) brain ECs in standard EC culture medium for eight days (see Materials and methods) and then performed RNA-seq and ATAC-seq on the resulting cells.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure used in the study.

claim: P-glycoprotein is expressed by CNS ECs but not by neurons, glia, or pericytes.
source: To selectively culture brain ECs, we took advantage of the expression of P-glycoprotein – an efflux pump with broad substrate specificity – by CNS ECs but not by neurons, glia, or pericytes.
evidence: This is stated as the basis for the selective culture method.

claim: Puromycin treatment kills non-ECs and selectively spares ECs in mixed brain cell cultures.
source: Following dissociation of brain cells and enrichment for vascular fragments, the mixed culture was treated with puromycin for 2–2.5 days, which kills non-ECs and selectively spares ECs, a widely used method for preparing pure cultures of acutely isolated CNS ECs (Figure 1A; Welser-Alves et al., 2014; Assmann et al., 2017; reviewed in Helms et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as an established method with supporting citations.

claim: Cultured EC monolayers show uniform expression of the pan-EC marker CD31 (PECAM1).
source: Immunostaining of the resulting EC cultures revealed uniform expression of the pan-EC marker CD31 (PECAM1) across the monolayer (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in the figure.

claim: 3585 protein-coding transcripts met criteria for differential expression between acutely isolated and cultured brain ECs.
source: In comparing acutely isolated versus cultured brain ECs, 3585 protein-coding transcripts met our criteria for differential expression (see Materials and methods): 1542 with a > 2 fold increase in abundance in acutely isolated ECs and 2043 with a > 2 fold increase in abundance in cultured ECs.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the RNA-seq analysis.

claim: 1542 protein-coding transcripts showed > 2 fold increase in abundance in acutely isolated ECs compared to cultured ECs.
source: In comparing acutely isolated versus cultured brain ECs, 3585 protein-coding transcripts met our criteria for differential expression (see Materials and methods): 1542 with a > 2 fold increase in abundance in acutely isolated ECs and 2043 with a > 2 fold increase in abundance in cultured ECs.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the RNA-seq analysis.

claim: 2043 protein-coding transcripts showed > 2 fold increase in abundance in cultured ECs compared to acutely isolated ECs.
source: In comparing acutely isolated versus cultured brain ECs, 3585 protein-coding transcripts met our criteria for differential expression (see Materials and methods): 1542 with a > 2 fold increase in abundance in acutely isolated ECs and 2043 with a > 2 fold increase in abundance in cultured ECs.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the RNA-seq analysis.

claim: Pan-EC transcripts are present at similar levels in acutely isolated and cultured adult brain ECs.
source: Scatter plots comparing between-sample normalized RNA-seq read counts for acutely isolated versus cultured adult brain ECs show that, on average, pan-EC transcripts are present at similar levels, whereas most BBB transcripts show reduced abundance in the cultured brain ECs [Figure 1B].
evidence: This is shown in the scatter plot analysis in Figure 1B.

claim: Most BBB transcripts show reduced abundance in cultured brain ECs compared to acutely isolated brain ECs.
source: Scatter plots comparing between-sample normalized RNA-seq read counts for acutely isolated versus cultured adult brain ECs show that, on average, pan-EC transcripts are present at similar levels, whereas most BBB transcripts show reduced abundance in the cultured brain ECs [Figure 1B].
evidence: This is shown in the scatter plot analysis in Figure 1B.

claim: With eight days in culture, CNS ECs retain the core EC transcriptional program but begin losing the CNS-specific transcriptional program.
source: This analysis indicates that, with eight days in culture, CNS ECs retain the core EC transcriptional program but begin losing the CNS-specific transcriptional program.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the RNA-seq data comparing pan-EC and BBB transcripts.

claim: Cultured adult brain ECs are more closely related to P7 and adult brain ECs than to P7 liver, lung, or kidney ECs based on tissue-specific gene expression.
source: A dendrogram of the relatedness of the different EC samples shows that cultured adult brain ECs are more closely related to P7 and adult brain ECs than to P7 liver, lung, or kidney ECs (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is shown in the dendrogram analysis in Figure 1C.

claim: Principal component analysis shows substantial divergence of the cultured brain EC transcriptome compared to the in vivo brain, liver, lung, and kidney EC transcriptomes.
source: Principal component analysis (PCA) of transcript abundances for all protein-coding genes shows substantial divergence of the cultured brain EC transcriptome compared to the in vivo brain, liver, lung, and kidney EC transcriptomes (upper panel of Figure 1D).
evidence: This is shown in the PCA analysis in Figure 1D.

claim: P7 and adult in vivo brain EC transcriptomes are closely similar.
source: This PCA also shows the close similarity of the P7 and adult in vivo brain EC transcriptomes.
evidence: This is observed in the PCA analysis.

claim: Cultured brain ECs showed reduced expression for some of the genes associated with the two capillary clusters.
source: The cultured brain ECs showed reduced expression for some of the genes associated with the two capillary clusters (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, 'Capillary-A' and 'Capillary-V' panels), consistent with the BBB program manifesting primarily at the capillary level.
evidence: This is shown in the scatter plot analysis comparing expression of capillary cluster genes.

claim: The BBB program manifests primarily at the capillary level.
source: The cultured brain ECs showed reduced expression for some of the genes associated with the two capillary clusters (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, 'Capillary-A' and 'Capillary-V' panels), consistent with the BBB program manifesting primarily at the capillary level.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the reduced expression of capillary cluster genes.

claim: Cultured brain ECs show an increase in expression of several genes associated with the mitotic cluster.
source: The cultured brain ECs also show an increase in expression of several genes associated with the mitotic cluster, consistent with the proliferation of ECs in culture (red arrow in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is shown in the scatter plot analysis in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The increase in expression of mitotic cluster genes in cultured brain ECs is consistent with the proliferation of ECs in culture.
source: The cultured brain ECs also show an increase in expression of several genes associated with the mitotic cluster, consistent with the proliferation of ECs in culture (red arrow in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the increased mitotic gene expression.

claim: 181 out of 279 BBB genes are reduced >2 fold in cultured brain ECs compared to acutely isolated brain ECs.
source: As noted above, cultured brain ECs maintain relatively high-level expression of generic EC transcripts, although with some variability from sample-to-sample, and they exhibit reduced expression of BBB genes (181/279 are reduced >2 fold; Figure 1B and Figure 1E).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the RNA-seq analysis.

claim: Genes known to be activated in response to beta-catenin signaling or whose protein products regulate beta-catenin signaling showed little or no expression in cultured brain ECs.
source: Genes known to be activated in response to beta-catenin signaling or whose protein products regulate beta-catenin signaling (Behrens et al., 1998; Shimomura et al., 2010; Chang and Sun, 2014; Kakugawa et al., 2015; Mazzoni et al., 2017) showed little or no expression in cultured brain ECs (Figure 1E), implying a lack of beta-catenin signaling under these culture conditions.
evidence: This is shown in the transcript abundance plots in Figure 1E.

claim: The low expression of beta-catenin-responsive genes in cultured brain ECs implies a lack of beta-catenin signaling under these culture conditions.
source: Genes known to be activated in response to beta-catenin signaling or whose protein products regulate beta-catenin signaling (Behrens et al., 1998; Shimomura et al., 2010; Chang and Sun, 2014; Kakugawa et al., 2015; Mazzoni et al., 2017) showed little or no expression in cultured brain ECs (Figure 1E), implying a lack of beta-catenin signaling under these culture conditions.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the gene expression data.

claim: Five beta-catenin-responsive genes (Apcdd1, Axin2, Lef1, Notum, and Spock2) also meet the criteria for inclusion as 'BBB genes'.
source: We note that five of these genes – Apcdd1, Axin2, Lef1, Notum, and Spock2 – also meet the criteria for inclusion as 'BBB genes', in accordance with the established role of beta-catenin signaling in CNS ECs.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the gene classification analysis.

claim: The overlap of beta-catenin-responsive genes with BBB genes is in accordance with the established role of beta-catenin signaling in CNS ECs.
source: We note that five of these genes – Apcdd1, Axin2, Lef1, Notum, and Spock2 – also meet the criteria for inclusion as 'BBB genes', in accordance with the established role of beta-catenin signaling in CNS ECs.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation consistent with established knowledge.

claim: Cldn5 transcripts show little change with in vitro culture.
source: Among the more abundant transcripts coding for TJ proteins there is a mixture of responses to in vitro culture: Cldn5 transcripts show little change, Lsr and Ocln transcripts are reduced ~2 fold, Jam2 and Tjp1 transcripts are reduced ~5 fold, and F11r and Tjp2 are elevated 2–4-fold in a subset of the cultured EC samples.
evidence: This is a result from the RNA-seq analysis of tight junction protein transcripts.

claim: Lsr and Ocln transcripts are reduced ~2 fold with in vitro culture.
source: Among the more abundant transcripts coding for TJ proteins there is a mixture of responses to in vitro culture: Cldn5 transcripts show little change, Lsr and Ocln transcripts are reduced ~2 fold, Jam2 and Tjp1 transcripts are reduced ~5 fold, and F11r and Tjp2 are elevated 2–4-fold in a subset of the cultured EC samples.
evidence: This is a result from the RNA-seq analysis of tight junction protein transcripts.

claim: Jam2 and Tjp1 transcripts are reduced ~5 fold with in vitro culture.
source: Among the more abundant transcripts coding for TJ proteins there is a mixture of responses to in vitro culture: Cldn5 transcripts show little change, Lsr and Ocln transcripts are reduced ~2 fold, Jam2 and Tjp1 transcripts are reduced ~5 fold, and F11r and Tjp2 are elevated 2–4-fold in a subset of the cultured EC samples.
evidence: This is a result from the RNA-seq analysis of tight junction protein transcripts.

claim: F11r and Tjp2 are elevated 2–4-fold in a subset of the cultured EC samples.
source: Among the more abundant transcripts coding for TJ proteins there is a mixture of responses to in vitro culture: Cldn5 transcripts show little change, Lsr and Ocln transcripts are reduced ~2 fold, Jam2 and Tjp1 transcripts are reduced ~5 fold, and F11r and Tjp2 are elevated 2–4-fold in a subset of the cultured EC samples.
evidence: This is a result from the RNA-seq analysis of tight junction protein transcripts.

claim: In vitro culture had either no effect or reduced expression of solute carrier family transporter transcripts.
source: Among transcripts coding for solute carrier family transporters, in vitro culture had either no effect (e.g., Slc16a9, Slc1a1, and Slc46a3) or it reduced expression, in several cases to a nearly undetectable levels (e.g., Slc22a8, Slc38a3, Slc39a10, and Slco1c1).
evidence: This is a result from the RNA-seq analysis of solute carrier transporter transcripts.

claim: In vitro culture reduced expression of Slc22a8, Slc38a3, Slc39a10, and Slco1c1 to nearly undetectable levels.
source: Among transcripts coding for solute carrier family transporters, in vitro culture had either no effect (e.g., Slc16a9, Slc1a1, and Slc46a3) or it reduced expression, in several cases to a nearly undetectable levels (e.g., Slc22a8, Slc38a3, Slc39a10, and Slco1c1).
evidence: This is a result from the RNA-seq analysis of solute carrier transporter transcripts.

claim: The levels of multiple transcripts coding for ABC transporters are either unaffected or elevated by in vitro culture.
source: The levels of multiple transcripts coding for ABC transporters are either unaffected (e.g., Abcc4 and Abcg2) or elevated (e.g., Abca3, Abcb1b, Abcc1, and Abce1) by in vitro culture; the one exception is the most abundant isoform of P-glycoprotein (Abcb1a), which is greatly reduced by in vitro culture.
evidence: This is a result from the RNA-seq analysis of ABC transporter transcripts.

claim: The most abundant isoform of P-glycoprotein (Abcb1a) is greatly reduced by in vitro culture.
source: The levels of multiple transcripts coding for ABC transporters are either unaffected (e.g., Abcc4 and Abcg2) or elevated (e.g., Abca3, Abcb1b, Abcc1, and Abce1) by in vitro culture; the one exception is the most abundant isoform of P-glycoprotein (Abcb1a), which is greatly reduced by in vitro culture.
evidence: This is a result from the RNA-seq analysis of ABC transporter transcripts.

claim: In vitro culture causes a dramatic reduction in the abundance of transcripts coding for the transcytosis regulator Mfsd2a.
source: Among transcytosis-associated transcripts, in vitro culture causes a dramatic reduction in the abundance of transcripts coding for the transcytosis regulator Mfsd2a (Figure 1E; Ben-Zvi et al., 2014) and concomitant increases in the abundances of transcripts coding for Caveolin-1, Caveolin-2, Cavin-1, Cavin-3, and Ehd2 (components of the Caveolin-mediated transcytotic pathway).
evidence: This is a result from the RNA-seq analysis with a supporting citation for Mfsd2a function.

claim: Mfsd2a is a transcytosis regulator.
source: Among transcytosis-associated transcripts, in vitro culture causes a dramatic reduction in the abundance of transcripts coding for the transcytosis regulator Mfsd2a (Figure 1E; Ben-Zvi et al., 2014)
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: In vitro culture causes concomitant increases in the abundances of transcripts coding for Caveolin-1, Caveolin-2, Cavin-1, Cavin-3, and Ehd2.
source: Among transcytosis-associated transcripts, in vitro culture causes a dramatic reduction in the abundance of transcripts coding for the transcytosis regulator Mfsd2a (Figure 1E; Ben-Zvi et al., 2014) and concomitant increases in the abundances of transcripts coding for Caveolin-1, Caveolin-2, Cavin-1, Cavin-3, and Ehd2 (components of the Caveolin-mediated transcytotic pathway).
evidence: This is a result from the RNA-seq analysis.

claim: Caveolin-1, Caveolin-2, Cavin-1, Cavin-3, and Ehd2 are components of the Caveolin-mediated transcytotic pathway.
source: Among transcytosis-associated transcripts, in vitro culture causes a dramatic reduction in the abundance of transcripts coding for the transcytosis regulator Mfsd2a (Figure 1E; Ben-Zvi et al., 2014) and concomitant increases in the abundances of transcripts coding for Caveolin-1, Caveolin-2, Cavin-1, Cavin-3, and Ehd2 (components of the Caveolin-mediated transcytotic pathway).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about these proteins.

claim: Among 16 transcripts coding for proteins associated with Clathrin-mediated transcytosis, only Clta and Cltb show consistent elevation with in vitro culture.
source: Among 16 transcripts coding for proteins associated with Clathrin-mediated transcytosis, only Clta and Cltb show consistent elevation with in vitro culture.
evidence: This is a result from the RNA-seq analysis.

claim: The broad reduction in the expression of beta-catenin-responsive and BBB genes implies a reduction in beta-catenin signaling and the BBB gene expression program in brain ECs cultured in vitro.
source: In summary, the broad reduction in the expression of beta-catenin-responsive and BBB genes implies a reduction in beta-catenin signaling and the BBB gene expression program in brain ECs cultured in vitro.
evidence: This is stated as a summary interpretation of the RNA-seq results.

claim: Comparisons of accessible chromatin in acutely isolated versus cultured brain ECs show loss of ATAC-seq peaks near multiple brain EC-specific genes that lose expression in cultured ECs.
source: Comparisons of accessible chromatin in acutely isolated versus cultured brain ECs show (1) loss of ATAC-seq peaks near multiple brain EC-specific genes that lose expression in cultured ECs, such as Slco1c1 and Mfsd2a, and (2) gain of ATAC-seq peaks near multiple genes that are induced in cultured ECs, such as Thbs1 and Cyr61 (also known as Ccn1) (Figure 2A; the histograms in the genome browser images represent averages of the independent replicates).
evidence: This is shown in the genome browser images in Figure 2A.

claim: Comparisons of accessible chromatin in acutely isolated versus cultured brain ECs show gain of ATAC-seq peaks near multiple genes that are induced in cultured ECs.
source: Comparisons of accessible chromatin in acutely isolated versus cultured brain ECs show (1) loss of ATAC-seq peaks near multiple brain EC-specific genes that lose expression in cultured ECs, such as Slco1c1 and Mfsd2a, and (2) gain of ATAC-seq peaks near multiple genes that are induced in cultured ECs, such as Thbs1 and Cyr61 (also known as Ccn1) (Figure 2A; the histograms in the genome browser images represent averages of the independent replicates).
evidence: This is shown in the genome browser images in Figure 2A.

claim: PCA of ATAC-seq read density indicates that the accessible chromatin landscapes of acutely isolated adult and P7 brain ECs are as different from cultured brain ECs as the latter is from peripheral ECs.
source: PCA of ATAC-seq read density at a consensus set of called ATAC-seq peaks indicates that the accessible chromatin landscapes of acutely isolated adult and P7 brain ECs are as different from cultured brain ECs as the latter is from peripheral ECs (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown in the PCA analysis in Figure 2B.

claim: Acutely isolated adult and P7 brain ECs have very similar accessible chromatin landscapes.
source: PCA also indicates that acutely isolated adult and P7 brain ECs have very similar accessible chromatin landscapes.
evidence: This is observed in the PCA analysis.

claim: Among 102,016 ATAC-seq peaks identified in the acutely isolated and cultured brain EC datasets, 16,760 were lost and 20,654 were gained as a result of in vitro culture.
source: Among 102,016 ATAC-seq peaks identified in the acutely isolated and cultured brain EC datasets, 16,760 were lost and 20,654 were gained as a result of in vitro culture (Figure 2C; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the ATAC-seq analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Accessible regions gained during in vitro culture were strongly enriched for motifs of the activator protein-1 (AP-1) complex (FOS, JUN, and ATF) and TEAD families.
source: Transcription factor (TF) motif enrichment analysis of ATAC-seq peaks revealed two distinctive trends: (1) accessible regions gained during in vitro culture were strongly enriched for motifs of the activator protein-1 (AP-1) complex (FOS, JUN, and ATF) and TEAD families, and (2) accessible regions lost during in vitro culture were strongly enriched for TCF/LEF, SOX, and SP/KLF motifs (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This is a result from the TF motif enrichment analysis shown in Figures 2D and E.

claim: Accessible regions lost during in vitro culture were strongly enriched for TCF/LEF, SOX, and SP/KLF motifs.
source: Transcription factor (TF) motif enrichment analysis of ATAC-seq peaks revealed two distinctive trends: (1) accessible regions gained during in vitro culture were strongly enriched for motifs of the activator protein-1 (AP-1) complex (FOS, JUN, and ATF) and TEAD families, and (2) accessible regions lost during in vitro culture were strongly enriched for TCF/LEF, SOX, and SP/KLF motifs (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This is a result from the TF motif enrichment analysis shown in Figures 2D and E.

claim: The AP1 and TEAD signatures in regions of gained open chromatin likely reflect cell proliferation and/or a stress response to the in vitro environment.
source: The AP1 and TEAD signatures in regions of gained open chromatin likely reflect cell proliferation and/or a stress response to the in vitro environment.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the motif enrichment data.

claim: The TCF/LEF signature in regions of open chromatin lost during in vitro culture likely reflects the loss of beta-catenin signaling under standard EC culture conditions.
source: The TCF/LEF signature in regions of open chromatin lost during in vitro culture likely reflects the loss of beta-catenin signaling under standard EC culture conditions.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the motif enrichment data.

claim: The SP/KLF signature in regions of open chromatin that are lost during in vitro culture could reflect the lack of laminar flow in the culture conditions.
source: The SP/KLF signature in regions of open chromatin that are lost during in vitro culture could reflect the lack of laminar flow in our culture conditions, as both Klf2 and Klf4 expression in ECs is induced by laminar flow (Atkins and Jain, 2007).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis with a supporting citation about Klf2 and Klf4 induction by flow.

claim: Both Klf2 and Klf4 expression in ECs is induced by laminar flow.
source: The SP/KLF signature in regions of open chromatin that are lost during in vitro culture could reflect the lack of laminar flow in our culture conditions, as both Klf2 and Klf4 expression in ECs is induced by laminar flow (Atkins and Jain, 2007).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: Both sets of accessible regions (gained and lost) show similar enrichment for motifs of the ETS family of TFs.
source: Both sets of accessible regions show similar enrichment for motifs of the ETS family of TFs, master regulators of EC development and function (Figure 2D and E; Shah et al., 2016), consistent with the maintenance of general EC markers in culture.
evidence: This is shown in the motif enrichment analysis in Figures 2D and E.

claim: ETS family TFs are master regulators of EC development and function.
source: Both sets of accessible regions show similar enrichment for motifs of the ETS family of TFs, master regulators of EC development and function (Figure 2D and E; Shah et al., 2016), consistent with the maintenance of general EC markers in culture.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: The similar enrichment for ETS motifs in both gained and lost accessible regions is consistent with the maintenance of general EC markers in culture.
source: Both sets of accessible regions show similar enrichment for motifs of the ETS family of TFs, master regulators of EC development and function (Figure 2D and E; Shah et al., 2016), consistent with the maintenance of general EC markers in culture.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the motif enrichment data.

claim: Cultured brain ECs showed reductions in the abundances of transcripts for brain EC-enriched TFs Lef1, Tcf7, and Zic3 relative to acutely isolated brain ECs.
source: Comparing the abundances of TF transcripts, Figure 2F shows that, relative to acutely isolated brain ECs, cultured brain ECs showed reductions in the abundances of transcripts for brain EC-enriched TFs Lef1, Tcf7, and Zic3, and increases in the abundances of transcripts for AP-1 family members Fosl2 and Jund (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is shown in the transcript abundance heatmap in Figure 2F.

claim: Cultured brain ECs showed increases in the abundances of transcripts for AP-1 family members Fosl2 and Jund relative to acutely isolated brain ECs.
source: Comparing the abundances of TF transcripts, Figure 2F shows that, relative to acutely isolated brain ECs, cultured brain ECs showed reductions in the abundances of transcripts for brain EC-enriched TFs Lef1, Tcf7, and Zic3, and increases in the abundances of transcripts for AP-1 family members Fosl2 and Jund (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is shown in the transcript abundance heatmap in Figure 2F.

claim: The down-regulation of transcripts coding for TFs such as Lef1, Tcf7, and Zic3 that mediate beta-catenin signaling could be both a consequence and a cause of reduced signaling by this pathway.
source: The down-regulation of transcripts coding for TFs such as Lef1, Tcf7, and Zic3 that mediate beta-catenin signaling could be both a consequence and a cause of reduced signaling by this pathway.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the TF expression changes.

claim: Transcripts coding for SP5, a direct target and downstream effector of beta-catenin signaling, are up-regulated in cultured ECs.
source: Interestingly, transcripts coding for SP5, a direct target and downstream effector of beta-catenin signaling (Weidinger et al., 2005; Fujimura et al., 2007), are up-regulated in cultured ECs, whereas transcripts coding for SP1, a widely expressed TF that recognizes the same SP/KLF motif, are down-regulated (arrows in Figure 2F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2F with supporting citations for SP5 function.

claim: SP5 and its close homologue SP8 mediate many of the effects of Wnt3a signaling on neural and mesodermal development during mammalian gastrulation.
source: Current evidence indicates that SP5 and its close homologue SP8 mediate many of the effects of Wnt3a signaling on neural and mesodermal development during mammalian gastrulation (Dunty et al., 2014; Kennedy et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: In HEK293T cells and human pluripotent stem cells, SP5 acts as a beta-catenin-inducible transcriptional repressor to inhibit the expression of genes that are activated by SP1.
source: In HEK293T cells and human pluripotent stem cells, SP5 acts as a beta-catenin-inducible transcriptional repressor to inhibit the expression of genes that are activated by SP1 (Fujimura et al., 2007; Huggins et al., 2017), and Huggins and colleagues have proposed that SP5 acts in the termination phase of beta-catenin signaling to repress beta-catenin target genes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: SP5 acts in the termination phase of beta-catenin signaling to repress beta-catenin target genes.
source: In HEK293T cells and human pluripotent stem cells, SP5 acts as a beta-catenin-inducible transcriptional repressor to inhibit the expression of genes that are activated by SP1 (Fujimura et al., 2007; Huggins et al., 2017), and Huggins and colleagues have proposed that SP5 acts in the termination phase of beta-catenin signaling to repress beta-catenin target genes.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis proposed by Huggins and colleagues.

claim: Pan-EC TF genes Erg, Fli1, and Ets1 show minimal changes in expression in cultured brain ECs.
source: Pan-EC TF genes Erg, Fli1, and Ets1 show minimal changes in expression in cultured brain ECs, consistent with the maintenance of general EC markers in culture.

claim: The minimal changes in expression of pan-EC TF genes in cultured brain ECs is consistent with the maintenance of general EC markers in culture.
source: Pan-EC TF genes Erg, Fli1, and Ets1 show minimal changes in expression in cultured brain ECs, consistent with the maintenance of general EC markers in culture.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the TF expression data.

claim: The data support the general inference from co-culture experiments that signals from the brain parenchyma are required to maintain the BBB state.
source: The data described thus far support the general inference from co-culture experiments with ECs and astrocytes, pericytes, and/or neurons that signals from the brain parenchyma are required to maintain the BBB state (Helms et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation consistent with previous co-culture experiments.

claim: Mouse genetic experiments show that a neuronal- and/or glial-derived beta-catenin signal is necessary for BBB development and maintenance in vivo.
source: More specifically, the data are consistent with mouse genetic experiments showing that a neuronal- and/or glial-derived beta-catenin signal is necessary for BBB development and maintenance in vivo, as summarized in the Introduction.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from mouse genetic experiments referenced in the Introduction.

claim: Cre-mediated excision of exon 3 of the beta-catenin gene (Ctnnb1) produces a constitutively active form of beta-catenin.
source: The strategy relies on Cre-mediated excision of exon 3 of the beta-catenin gene (Ctnnb1), which encompasses the sites of phosphorylation that lead to beta-catenin ubiquitination and degradation (Figure 3A; Harada et al., 1999; the allele with loxP sites flanking exon 3 is referred to as Ctnnb1flex3).
evidence: This is stated as the basis for the genetic strategy with a supporting citation.

claim: Exon 3 of Ctnnb1 encompasses the sites of phosphorylation that lead to beta-catenin ubiquitination and degradation.
source: The strategy relies on Cre-mediated excision of exon 3 of the beta-catenin gene (Ctnnb1), which encompasses the sites of phosphorylation that lead to beta-catenin ubiquitination and degradation (Figure 3A; Harada et al., 1999; the allele with loxP sites flanking exon 3 is referred to as Ctnnb1flex3).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: Cre-mediated recombination of Ctnnb1flex3 in ECs using Pdgfb-CreER and 4HT produces ~80% efficient recombination.
source: In previous work, Cre-mediated recombination of Ctnnb1flex3 in ECs was induced in vivo using a Pdgfb-CreER transgene and intraperitoneal injection of 4-hydroxytamoxifen (4HT), a procedure that reliably produces ~80% efficient recombination, as determined by the partial conversion of CVO and choroid plexus ECs from a BBB-deficient to a BBB-proficient state (Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a result from previous work with a supporting citation.

claim: RNA-seq reads spanning Ctnnb1 exons 2+4 are only present in the genotype carrying the Pdgfb-CreER and Ctnnb1flex3 alleles.
source: A comparison of RNA-seq read counts from brain ECs cultured from wild-type (WT) control (either C57BL/6J or Ctnnb1flex3/+;Tie2-GFP) injected with 100 ug 4HT at P10 and Ctnnb1flex3/+;Pdgfb-CreER;Tie2-GFP mice injected with 100 ug 4HT at P10 reveals reads spanning Ctnnb1 exons 2+4 only in the genotype carrying the Pdgfb-CreER and Ctnnb1flex3 alleles, implying that cultured brain ECs contain the exon 3 deleted transcripts that code for stabilized beta-catenin (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is shown in the RNA-seq analysis in Figure 3B.

claim: Cultured brain ECs from Ctnnb1flex3/+;Pdgfb-CreER;Tie2-GFP mice contain the exon 3 deleted transcripts that code for stabilized beta-catenin.
source: A comparison of RNA-seq read counts from brain ECs cultured from wild-type (WT) control (either C57BL/6J or Ctnnb1flex3/+;Tie2-GFP) injected with 100 ug 4HT at P10 and Ctnnb1flex3/+;Pdgfb-CreER;Tie2-GFP mice injected with 100 ug 4HT at P10 reveals reads spanning Ctnnb1 exons 2+4 only in the genotype carrying the Pdgfb-CreER and Ctnnb1flex3 alleles, implying that cultured brain ECs contain the exon 3 deleted transcripts that code for stabilized beta-catenin (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the RNA-seq data.

claim: Expression of the exon 3 deleted allele of Ctnnb1 had virtually no effect on the transcriptional profile of cultured brain ECs.
source: Surprisingly, scatter plots comparing between-sample normalized RNA-seq read counts for WT versus beta-catenin stabilized cultured brain ECs show that expression of the exon 3 deleted allele of Ctnnb1 had virtually no effect on the transcriptional profile of cultured brain ECs, and, in particular, had virtually no effect on either pan-EC transcripts or BBB transcripts (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown in the scatter plot analysis in Figure 3C.

claim: Expression of the exon 3 deleted allele of Ctnnb1 had virtually no effect on pan-EC transcripts or BBB transcripts in cultured brain ECs.
source: Surprisingly, scatter plots comparing between-sample normalized RNA-seq read counts for WT versus beta-catenin stabilized cultured brain ECs show that expression of the exon 3 deleted allele of Ctnnb1 had virtually no effect on the transcriptional profile of cultured brain ECs, and, in particular, had virtually no effect on either pan-EC transcripts or BBB transcripts (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown in the scatter plot analysis in Figure 3C.

claim: The expression of six genes regulated by beta-catenin signaling and Tcf7 were extremely low in beta-catenin stabilized cultured brain ECs.
source: Moreover, the expression of the six genes regulated by beta-catenin signaling that were shown in Figure 1E, and a seventh (Tcf7) were extremely low in beta-catenin stabilized cultured brain ECs (Figure 3D), implying a failure to activate beta-catenin signaling despite production of stabilized beta-catenin.
evidence: This is shown in the transcript abundance plots in Figure 3D.

claim: The extremely low expression of beta-catenin-responsive genes in beta-catenin stabilized cultured brain ECs implies a failure to activate beta-catenin signaling despite production of stabilized beta-catenin.
source: Moreover, the expression of the six genes regulated by beta-catenin signaling that were shown in Figure 1E, and a seventh (Tcf7) were extremely low in beta-catenin stabilized cultured brain ECs (Figure 3D), implying a failure to activate beta-catenin signaling despite production of stabilized beta-catenin.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the gene expression data.

claim: PCA indicates that beta-catenin stabilized cultured brain ECs are virtually identical to their WT counterparts.
source: PCA of transcript abundances for all protein-coding genes and PCA of all called ATAC-seq peaks also indicates that beta-catenin stabilized cultured brain ECs are virtually identical to their WT counterparts (Figure 3E, cyan and black arrows).
evidence: This is shown in the PCA analysis in Figure 3E.

claim: Under the conventional in vitro culture conditions employed, CNS ECs become refractory to the effects of beta-catenin stabilization.
source: The simplest interpretation of these findings is that under the conventional in vitro culture conditions employed here, CNS ECs become refractory to the effects of beta-catenin stabilization.
evidence: This is stated as the simplest interpretation of the beta-catenin stabilization results.

claim: Neural tissue induces a BBB/BRB gene expression program in ECs that invade from the surrounding perineural vascular plexus.
source: In the case of CNS vascular development, neural tissue induces a BBB/BRB gene expression program in ECs that invade from the surrounding perineural vascular plexus (Feeney and Watterson, 1946; Stewart and Wiley, 1981).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: An essential component of the BBB/BRB instructive signal is beta-catenin signaling, induced by neuron- and/or glia-derived ligands.
source: As noted in the Introduction, gene knockout studies in mice have demonstrated that an essential component of this BBB/BRB instructive signal is beta-catenin signaling, induced by neuron- and/or glia-derived ligands (Liebner et al., 2008; Stenman et al., 2008; Daneman et al., 2009; Wang et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2014; Cho et al., 2017; Benz et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from gene knockout studies with supporting citations.

claim: LEF1 and TCF7 are present in CNS ECs but not in non-CNS ECs.
source: Two additional pieces of evidence that underscore the central role of beta-catenin signaling in CNS EC-specific gene regulation are: (1) the presence in CNS ECs, but not in non-CNS ECs, of LEF1 and TCF7, members of the TCF/LEF family of transcription factors (TFs) that both mediate and are induced by the beta-catenin signal
evidence: This is stated as evidence for the role of beta-catenin signaling in CNS ECs.

claim: LEF1 and TCF7 are members of the TCF/LEF family of transcription factors that both mediate and are induced by the beta-catenin signal.

evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about LEF1 and TCF7 function.

evidence: This is stated as evidence from previous work with a supporting citation.

claim: The rapid reduction in the abundance of many BBB transcripts in short-term cultures of brain ECs is correlated with reduced beta-catenin signaling.
source: In short-term cultures of brain ECs, the present work reveals that the rapid reduction in the abundance of many BBB transcripts is correlated with reduced beta-catenin signaling.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the present work.

source: In contrast, the expression of generic EC genes, such as Cd31/Pecam1, is minimally affected.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the present work.

source: The reduction in beta-catenin signaling in culture is seen at both the transcriptional and chromatin accessibility levels.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the RNA-seq and ATAC-seq findings.

claim: Multiple genes that are known beta-catenin targets and that are expressed in acutely isolated brain ECs are not detectably expressed or are expressed at extremely low levels in cultured brain ECs.
source: For example, multiple genes that are known beta-catenin targets and that are expressed in acutely isolated brain ECs are not detectably expressed or are expressed at extremely low levels in cultured brain ECs.
evidence: This is stated as an example of reduced beta-catenin signaling in culture.

claim: Cultured brain ECs retain the expression of generic EC TF genes such as Erg, Ets1, and Fli1.
source: Furthermore, while cultured brain ECs retain the expression of generic EC TF genes such as Erg, Ets1, and Fli1, the drastic reduction in expression of Lef1 and Tcf7, which are both mediators and targets of beta-catenin signaling, likely contributes to the reduced response of cultured ECs to beta-catenin stabilization.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the RNA-seq analysis.

claim: The drastic reduction in expression of Lef1 and Tcf7 likely contributes to the reduced response of cultured ECs to beta-catenin stabilization.

evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Lef1 and Tcf7.

claim: Under low beta-catenin signaling and no blood flow culture conditions, brain ECs utilize ETS family TFs in conjunction with AP1 and TEAD TFs to promote proliferation.
source: One simple model for the difference between in vivo and in vitro patterns of gene expression is that under low beta-catenin signaling and no blood flow culture conditions, brain ECs utilize ETS family TFs in conjunction with AP1 and TEAD TFs to promote proliferation, whereas under the high beta-catenin signaling and normal blood flow conditions of the in vivo CNS, ETS TFs collaborate with SP/KLF, TCF/LEF, and ZIC factors to promote BBB gene expression.
evidence: This is stated as a model to explain the differences between in vivo and in vitro gene expression.

claim: Under high beta-catenin signaling and normal blood flow conditions of the in vivo CNS, ETS TFs collaborate with SP/KLF, TCF/LEF, and ZIC factors to promote BBB gene expression.
source: One simple model for the difference between in vivo and in vitro patterns of gene expression is that under low beta-catenin signaling and no blood flow culture conditions, brain ECs utilize ETS family TFs in conjunction with AP1 and TEAD TFs to promote proliferation, whereas under the high beta-catenin signaling and normal blood flow conditions of the in vivo CNS, ETS TFs collaborate with SP/KLF, TCF/LEF, and ZIC factors to promote BBB gene expression.
evidence: This is stated as a model to explain the differences between in vivo and in vitro gene expression.

claim: The lability of the BBB program in vitro is reminiscent of earlier experiments in which acute loss of EC beta-catenin signaling in vivo led to a loss of BBB markers and a loss of barrier integrity.
source: The lability of the BBB program in vitro is reminiscent of earlier experiments in which acute loss of EC beta-catenin signaling in vivo led to a loss of BBB markers and a loss of barrier integrity (Liebner et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to previous in vivo experiments with supporting citations.

claim: Previous work with cultured brain ECs and with immortalized CNS EC lines has shown that activating beta-catenin signaling with Wnt ligands, small molecule agonists, or by genetic means can enhance the expression of genes specific to the BBB.
source: Previous work with cultured brain ECs and with immortalized CNS EC lines has shown that activating beta-catenin signaling with Wnt ligands, small molecule agonists, or by genetic means can enhance the expression of genes specific to the BBB (Paolinelli et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as previous work with a supporting citation.

claim: Paolinelli and colleagues observed relatively modest effects of beta-catenin stabilization on BBB gene expression.
source: While our data appear to be at odds with the data of Paolinelli et al. (2013), we note that Paollinelli and colleagues observed relatively modest effects of beta-catenin stabilization, and they did not include acutely isolated CNS ECs in their comparisons, leaving open the possibility that the transcriptional effects they observed were minor compared to the differences between in vivo and in vitro transcriptional programs.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to the work of Paolinelli et al.

claim: One or more additional signaling pathways gate the beta-catenin signal in CNS ECs and the relevant signals for these other pathways are missing from the in vitro culture system.
source: Based on our genome-wide transcriptional and chromatin accessibility analyses, we suggest that one or more additional signaling pathways gate the beta-catenin signal in CNS ECs and that the relevant signals for these other pathways are missing from the in vitro culture system.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis based on the study findings.

claim: During normal development ECs encounter additional signals in the CNS that render them receptive to the beta-catenin signal.
source: If correct, this model implies that during normal development ECs encounter additional signals in the CNS that render them receptive to the beta-catenin signal.
evidence: This is stated as an implication of the proposed model.

claim: The present study demonstrates the utility of applying genome-wide transcriptional and chromatin accessibility profiling to the characterization of ECs in culture.
source: Finally, the present study serves as a demonstration of the utility of applying genome-wide transcriptional and chromatin accessibility profiling to the characterization of ECs in culture.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion about the methodological approach.

claim: The combination of transcriptional and chromatin accessibility profiling has been used previously to distinguish tumor and immune cell subtypes.
source: This combination of approaches has been used previously to distinguish tumor and immune cell subtypes (Corces et al., 2018; Satpathy et al., 2019), and it should be useful in defining the differentiation state of CNS ECs grown under different culture or co-culture conditions or in the presence of candidate signaling molecules.
evidence: This is stated as previous applications of the method with supporting citations.
